meta.title: Enterprise Integration Backbone
meta.summary: Replace brittle point-to-point scripts between an ERP, a CRM, an online shop and a warehouse system with managed APIs, canonical business events on a shared backbone, one connector per system, and the retries, dedup and replay that keep an order from being lost or booked twice.

functional: Send every online and partner order to the ERP, the warehouse system and the CRM without point-to-point scripts
Propagate customer changes between the CRM, the ERP and the shop, following which system owns which field
Publish inventory adjustments from the warehouse system to the shop and the ERP
Expose versioned synchronous APIs (create order, order status) to partners and internal apps, with auth and quotas
Retry failed deliveries, dead-letter what cannot be delivered, and let an operator replay it safely
Follow any order across all systems by one correlation id
nonFunctional: An order reaches the ERP, WMS and CRM within 5 minutes for 99% of orders; any order missing from the ERP after 15 minutes raises an alert
No lost orders and no duplicate sales orders, across retries, redeliveries, replays and outages
Events for one business key (order, customer, SKU) are applied in the order they happened
Partner APIs: 99.9% availability and < 300 ms p99
Ride out a 6-hour ERP maintenance window with no data loss and no manual re-entry
A schema change never breaks an existing consumer

scale.label: Orders
scale.value: ~20,000/day average, 100,000 on peak days (~3.5/s in the busiest hour)

scale.label: Business events
scale.value: ~400,000/day (≈5/s average): order lifecycle 120k, inventory adjustments 200k, customer 30k, product and price 50k

scale.label: Peak event rate
scale.value: ~300/s during Black Friday hours and warehouse wave releases; backbone sized for 1,000/s

scale.label: Partner API
scale.value: ~2M calls/day from ~15 partners and internal apps, 200 requests/s peak

scale.label: ERP outage backlog
scale.value: 6 h window ≈ 5,000 orders plus 7,500 customer events (12,500 at the daily averages); drained at 20/s in ~10 min

scale.label: Salesforce API budget
scale.value: 100,000 calls per 24 h plus 1,000 per user licence; integration may use 60% of it

slos.name: Orders reach every system
slos.sli: Orders whose tracking row has ERP, WMS and CRM timestamps within the threshold of OrderPlaced, divided by all orders, from the order tracking table

slos.name: Partner API availability
slos.sli: Partner and internal API requests answered without a 5xx, divided by all requests, at API management

slos.name: Partner API latency
slos.sli: Partner and internal API requests answered within the threshold, divided by all requests, measured at API management (integration latency included)

slos.name: Every order booked exactly once
slos.sli: Shop orders that match exactly one ERP sales order by external reference, divided by all shop orders, in the nightly reconciliation

alerts.when: Any order placed more than 15 minutes ago with no ERP booking, outside an announced maintenance window
alerts.why: This is the symptom the business feels: the warehouse may ship it but finance never invoices it, or nobody ships it at all. It catches failures that no technical metric shows, such as a mapping that silently drops orders.

alerts.when: Partner API errors burning the error budget 14.4 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
alerts.why: Partners cannot place or track orders, and their own systems start retrying on top of the outage.

alerts.when: More than 1% of partner API requests slower than 300 ms, over 10 minutes and over 1 hour
alerts.why: Partners' own timeouts start firing and they retry, which adds load. Usually the integration store or a synchronous status lookup is slow.

alerts.when: Partner API errors burning the error budget 2 times too fast over 6 hours and 3 days
alerts.why: A small steady error rate, often one partner's bad requests or one route, that never pages but uses up the month's budget.

alerts.when: ERP connector lag above 2,000 events or oldest unprocessed event older than 10 minutes, for 10 minutes
alerts.why: Lag is the cause that comes before stale orders. A ticket, because inside a maintenance window it is expected and the stale order alert pages if it matters.

alerts.when: Any new message on a dead-letter topic, or any dead-letter message older than 24 hours
alerts.why: Every dead-lettered message is a business record that did not arrive somewhere, and it also blocks later events for the same key.

alerts.when: Salesforce API usage above 70% of the rolling 24-hour allowance
alerts.why: When the allowance runs out, every integration and every user tool calling the API fails until the window rolls, so slow down and batch before that happens.

alerts.when: Nightly reconciliation finds a shop order with no ERP sales order, or with more than one
alerts.why: A missing order is lost revenue and a duplicate is a double shipment or double invoice. Both mean a dedup or tracking bug that must be found before it repeats.

alerts.when: Any connector's OAuth client secret or certificate (SAP, Salesforce, shop, WMS), or the shop webhook secret, expires within 21 days without a rotated successor
alerts.why: An expired credential stops one integration completely, and it is the most common cause of a quiet Monday outage. Rotation is automated, so this catches rotation that failed.

signals.name: Lag and circuit state
signals.why: Shows whether the connector is behind because SAP is slow, down, or one partition is stuck on a single key.

signals.name: Salesforce API allowance left
signals.why: The org-wide limit is shared with every other tool, so read it on every response rather than counting your own calls.

signals.name: Mapping failures by reason
signals.why: An unknown SKU usually means a product was created in the shop before the ERP, which is a master data process problem, not a code bug.

signals.name: Dead-letter depth per consumer
signals.why: Tells you which connector is failing and for how long.

signals.name: Dedup outcomes
signals.why: A rise in duplicates means redeliveries or replays; in_doubt means a side effect whose result was lost and had to be looked up in the target.

signals.name: Rejected schema changes
signals.why: A producer trying to register a breaking change is caught here, before any consumer sees it.

signals.name: Orders booked in the ERP per hour against last week
signals.why: The business view: a drop with no errors anywhere usually means a mapping or filter is silently skipping orders.

debug.symptom: A customer says order SHOP-1002 was confirmed but never shipped
steps: Look up SHOP-1002 in the order tracking table: it shows the correlation id and which systems have stamped it (received, ERP, WMS, CRM) and when.
For the first missing stage, check that connector's dead-letter topic and its parked keys for the order id, and its consumer lag on the order's partition.
If nothing is parked, search the logs and traces of every connector by the correlation id to see the last hop that handled it.
Ask the target system directly by the external reference (PurchaseOrderByCustomer in SAP, clientOrderRef in the WMS): the order may exist with the tracking update lost.
Fix the cause, then replay the parked event to that one consumer, never to the main topic.

debug.symptom: ERP connector lag keeps growing although SAP is up
steps: Check whether the lag is on every partition or on one: one partition means one key is blocked or one message is slow.
Look at the circuit state and SAP response times; rising latency means SAP work processes are saturated, so lower the drain rate rather than adding consumers.
Check for a parked key at the head of the stuck partition and whether its fix needs a replay.
Only add consumers if partitions outnumber them, since one partition is processed by one consumer at a time.

nodes.label: Internal Load Balancer (L7)
nodes.description: Private, in the app subnets across three zones. API management reaches it through a private integration (a VPC link on AWS, Private Service Connect from Apigee); it routes /hooks and partner order paths to the commerce adapter and /ops to integration ops, and health-checks every task

nodes.label: Partner and Internal Apps
nodes.description: B2B partners and marketplaces, the customer service portal, the integration support console

nodes.label: DNS
nodes.description: Points api.acme.example (partner APIs, webhooks, ops API) at API management

nodes.label: API Management
nodes.description: Partner and internal APIs: OAuth, API keys, per-partner quotas, versioned routes; the public endpoint for webhooks. A web application firewall sits on it (AWS WAF on the API Gateway REST API stage, Cloud Armor in front of Apigee), and it reaches the services only through a private integration to the internal load balancer

nodes.label: Commerce Adapter
nodes.description: Shop webhooks and partner order APIs in, canonical OrderPlaced out; pushes customer and stock changes back to the shop

nodes.label: Integration Ops
nodes.description: Business monitor (stale orders every 5 min), nightly reconciliation, dead-letter browser and replay API

nodes.label: Integration Store
nodes.description: processed_events (dedup), id_xref (ids across systems), order_tracking, applied_versions, parked_keys

nodes.label: Schema Registry
nodes.description: Avro schemas for the canonical events with BACKWARD compatibility enforced; producers register and look up schema ids, consumers decode by the id in each message

nodes.label: Event Backbone
nodes.description: Canonical topics (OrderPlaced, CustomerUpdated, InventoryAdjusted) keyed by business id, 12 partitions, 7-day retention; retry and dead-letter topics per consumer; every event is serialized against a schema in the schema registry

nodes.label: ERP Connector
nodes.description: Consumer group erp-connector: books sales orders and updates business partners in SAP over OData, with a circuit breaker

nodes.label: WMS Connector
nodes.description: Consumer group wms-connector: creates outbound orders; polls the WMS stock movements API every minute and publishes InventoryAdjusted

nodes.label: CRM Connector
nodes.description: Subscribes to Salesforce Change Data Capture and publishes CustomerUpdated; upserts orders into Salesforce by external id

nodes.label: E-commerce Platform
nodes.description: SaaS shop (for example Shopify or Adobe Commerce): sends signed webhooks, accepts admin API calls

nodes.label: ERP (SAP S/4HANA)
nodes.description: System of record for products, prices, billing and credit; sales orders become invoices here. Reached over a site-to-site VPN or private connection, never the open internet; the SaaS systems (shop, WMS, Salesforce) are called through the NAT gateways

nodes.label: Warehouse System
nodes.description: Owns stock on hand and shipping: picks, packs and ships outbound orders

nodes.label: CRM (Salesforce)
nodes.description: Owns customer contact details, consent and sales activity

flows.title: Online order reaches ERP, WMS and CRM
flows.summary: The shop's webhook becomes one canonical OrderPlaced event keyed by order id. Three connectors consume it independently, each deduplicating and booking the order in its own system with the order id as the external reference.

steps.label: POST /hooks/shop/orders-create
steps.detail: The shop pushes the new order as a signed webhook instead of the old script polling it every 15 minutes, so the order enters the backbone within seconds.
steps.payload:
POST /hooks/shop/orders-create HTTP/1.1
X-Shopify-Topic: orders/create
X-Shopify-Webhook-Id: b54557e4-bdd9-4b37-8a5f-bf7d70bcd043
X-Shopify-Hmac-Sha256: XWmrwMey6OsLMeiZKwP4FppHH3cmAiiJJAweH5Jo4bM=

{ "id": 820982911946154508, "name": "#1001", "email": "ana@example.com", "currency": "EUR", "total_price": "129.90",
  "line_items": [ { "sku": "TSHIRT-BLK-M", "quantity": 2, "price": "39.95" }, { "sku": "HOODIE-GRY-L", "quantity": 1, "price": "50.00" } ] }

steps.label: forward raw body
steps.detail: The web application firewall on the gateway checks managed rules and request size first; the gateway then applies a rate limit and passes the body through byte for byte, because the signature is computed over the raw bytes. It reaches the private load balancer through its VPC link, so no service has a public address.
steps.payload:
POST /hooks/shop/orders-create HTTP/1.1
X-Shopify-Hmac-Sha256: XWmrwMey6OsLMeiZKwP4FppHH3cmAiiJJAweH5Jo4bM=
traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
(raw body unchanged)

steps.label: route /hooks/* to a commerce task
steps.detail: The internal load balancer picks a healthy task in any zone by path. The gateway starts a trace here, and the adapter copies its traceparent into the event headers, so the whole order is one trace.

steps.label: verify HMAC signature
steps.detail: An HMAC with the shop's shared secret, loaded from the secrets manager, proves the shop sent it. Anything unsigned is rejected before it can become a business event.

steps.label: look up ids, start tracking
steps.detail: The cross-reference table turns the shop's customer and SKUs into canonical ids, and the tracking row is the start of the order's trail across systems. The upsert makes a repeated webhook harmless.

steps.label: map to canonical OrderPlaced
steps.detail: Prices become integer minor units, SKUs and the customer become canonical ids, and only the fields other systems need are kept. Shop-only details such as theme or discount script ids stay out of the canonical event.

steps.label: serialize with OrderPlaced v3 (schema 47)
steps.detail: The Avro serializer looks the schema id up in the registry once and caches it, and the id travels in every message so consumers can decode it. Registering a breaking change fails here, in the producer, before any consumer sees it.

steps.label: produce key=SHOP-1001, acks=all
steps.detail: Keying by order id puts every event for this order on one partition, so OrderCancelled can never overtake OrderPlaced. The event id is derived from the shop's order id, so a repeated webhook produces the same id and consumers drop it.
steps.payload:
topic: orders.order-placed   key: SHOP-1001
headers: ce_id=evt-shop-820982911946154508-placed, ce_type=OrderPlaced, ce_source=shop,
         correlation_id=SHOP-1001, traceparent=00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
value (Avro, schema 47):
{ "orderId": "SHOP-1001", "customerId": "cus_58213", "channel": "web", "currency": "EUR", "totalMinor": 12990,
  "lines": [ { "sku": "TSHIRT-BLK-M", "qty": 2, "unitPriceMinor": 3995 }, { "sku": "HOODIE-GRY-L", "qty": 1, "unitPriceMinor": 5000 } ],
  "placedAt": "2026-11-10T09:14:03Z" }

steps.label: partition 7, offset 88213
steps.detail: acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 means the event is on every in-sync replica, at least two of the three brokers in different zones, before the adapter answers the shop.

steps.label: 200 OK
steps.detail: Answer only after the backbone has the event. If anything failed, a 5xx makes the shop retry for hours, so the shop's retry is the safety net for this hop.

steps.label: OrderPlaced (group erp-connector)
steps.detail: Each connector is its own consumer group with its own offsets, so a slow or down ERP never holds up the warehouse.

steps.label: claim event id
steps.detail: The unique key on (consumer, event id) turns at-least-once delivery into effectively-once processing for this connector. If nothing comes back, the row already exists and the connector reads its status: done means skip, in_progress means an earlier attempt is in doubt.
steps.payload:
INSERT INTO processed_events (consumer, event_id, status, started_at)
VALUES ('erp-connector', 'evt-shop-820982911946154508-placed', 'in_progress', now())
ON CONFLICT (consumer, event_id) DO NOTHING
RETURNING status;

steps.label: POST A_SalesOrder
steps.detail: The shop order id goes into PurchaseOrderByCustomer, so the order can always be found in SAP by our reference. The connector authenticates with an OAuth client credentials token for a technical user that may only create sales orders and change business partners.
steps.payload:
POST /sap/opu/odata/sap/API_SALES_ORDER_SRV/A_SalesOrder
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci... (client credentials, scope API_SALES_ORDER_SRV)

{ "SalesOrderType": "OR", "SalesOrganization": "1010", "DistributionChannel": "10", "OrganizationDivision": "00",
  "SoldToParty": "17100001", "PurchaseOrderByCustomer": "SHOP-1001",
  "to_Item": [ { "Material": "100045", "RequestedQuantity": "2" }, { "Material": "100212", "RequestedQuantity": "1" } ] }

steps.label: mark done, save xref, stamp tracking
steps.detail: Recording the SAP number lets later events (cancel, return) find the sales order, and the tracking stamp is what the business monitor watches.

steps.label: commit offset 88213
steps.detail: The offset is committed after the side effect, never before. A crash in between means the event comes again, and the done row makes the repeat a no-op.

steps.label: OrderPlaced (group wms-connector)
steps.detail: The warehouse gets the order in parallel with the ERP. That is choreography: nobody waits for the ERP before picking can start.

steps.label: POST /outbound-orders
steps.detail: The WMS rejects a second order with the same client reference with 409, so a redelivered event cannot create a second shipment.

steps.label: OrderPlaced (group crm-connector)
steps.detail: Sales and service teams see the order on the customer's record, which the old nightly export showed a day late.

steps.label: upsert Order by Shop_Order_Id__c
steps.detail: An upsert keyed by an external id field is idempotent by design: a repeat updates the same record instead of inserting a second one.

steps.label: mark done, stamp crm_at
steps.detail: With all three stamps set about 4 seconds after the webhook, the order counts as propagated for the SLO.

flows.title: Customer update in the CRM propagates in order
flows.summary: A sales rep changes a customer's email in Salesforce. Change Data Capture feeds the CRM connector, which publishes only the fields the CRM owns, keyed by customer id, and each target applies it only if it is newer than what it already has.

steps.label: AccountChangeEvent (Pub/Sub API)
steps.detail: The connector holds a subscription to Salesforce Change Data Capture and stores the last replay id, so after a restart it resumes where it stopped instead of polling for changes. Salesforce keeps change events for 72 hours, so an outage longer than that needs a resync of the affected records.

steps.label: drop echoes, keep owned fields
steps.detail: Changes made by the integration's own user are dropped, otherwise an ERP update written into Salesforce would come straight back as a new event and loop forever. Only fields the CRM owns (email, phone, consent) go on; a billing address edited here is ignored because the ERP owns it.

steps.label: xref Salesforce id to canonical id
steps.detail: Every system has its own customer id. The cross-reference table is what lets one event address the same customer in all of them.
steps.payload:
SELECT canonical_id FROM id_xref
WHERE entity = 'customer' AND system = 'salesforce' AND system_id = '001Hn00001xYzAbIAK';

steps.label: serialize with CustomerUpdated v2
steps.detail: Serializing against the registered schema means a field renamed in a connector deploy fails here, in the producer, instead of in three consumers.

steps.label: produce key=cus_58213
steps.detail: Keyed by canonical customer id, so two quick edits to the same customer land on one partition in commit order. The source version travels with the event for the targets' stale check.
steps.payload:
topic: customers.customer-updated   key: cus_58213
headers: ce_type=CustomerUpdated, ce_source=salesforce, correlation_id=cus_58213
value (Avro, schema 52):
{ "customerId": "cus_58213", "sourceVersion": 11850391245013,
  "changed": { "email": "ana.ruiz@example.com" }, "changedAt": "2026-11-10T09:15:00Z" }

steps.label: last applied version for cus_58213
steps.detail: Partition order covers normal delivery, but a replay or a retry topic can bring an older change after a newer one. Comparing versions makes applying it again or late harmless.

steps.label: PATCH business partner email
steps.detail: Only the changed field is sent, so the update cannot overwrite fields SAP owns, such as credit limit or billing address.

steps.label: save applied version
steps.payload:
INSERT INTO applied_versions (consumer, entity_key, version)
VALUES ('erp-connector', 'cus_58213', 11850391245013)
ON CONFLICT (consumer, entity_key) DO UPDATE SET version = EXCLUDED.version
WHERE applied_versions.version < EXCLUDED.version;

steps.label: CustomerUpdated cus_58213
steps.detail: The commerce adapter is also the shop's inbound connector, so the email the customer logs in with matches the CRM.

steps.label: version check, shop customer id
steps.detail: Same stale check as the ERP, plus the shop's own id for this customer.

steps.label: PUT customer 7408005
steps.detail: The shop will fire a customers/update webhook for this change. The adapter recognises its own write by comparing against the values it just sent and does not publish it again.

flows.title: ERP down for maintenance: retry, dead-letter, replay
flows.summary: SAP goes into a planned 4-hour window while an order is in flight. The connector retries, dead-letters the one order whose outcome is unknown, pauses so the rest wait safely in the backbone, and after SAP returns an operator replays the order, which the connector finds already booked.

steps.label: OrderPlaced SHOP-1002
steps.detail: 02:00:00, the announced SAP maintenance window starts while the connector is working through the order topic.

steps.label: POST A_SalesOrder SHOP-1002
steps.detail: Same call as the happy path, with SHOP-1002 as PurchaseOrderByCustomer.

steps.label: timeout after 30 s
steps.detail: A timeout is not a failure. SAP may have saved the order just before shutting down, so the outcome is unknown.

steps.label: back off 5 s, 30 s, 2 min with jitter
steps.detail: Short outages and deploys clear within these retries. Jitter stops every connector instance from hitting SAP at the same moment when it comes back.

steps.label: GET by PurchaseOrderByCustomer
steps.detail: After an unknown outcome, every retry looks for the order before creating it. Creating blindly is how duplicate sales orders happen.

steps.label: produce to orders.erp-connector.dlq
steps.detail: The message moves aside with its full context, so the partition is not blocked by one order and an operator can see exactly what failed and why.
steps.payload:
topic: orders.erp-connector.dlq   key: SHOP-1002
headers: ce_id=evt-shop-820982911947201133-placed, correlation_id=SHOP-1002,
         dlq_source=orders.order-placed/7/88540, dlq_error=SocketTimeout, dlq_attempts=4,
         dlq_first_failed=2026-11-11T02:00:31Z, dlq_outcome=unknown
value: (original bytes, unchanged)

steps.label: park key SHOP-1002
steps.detail: While SHOP-1002 is parked, any later event for the same order, such as OrderCancelled, goes to the same dead-letter topic behind it instead of to SAP, otherwise the cancel would reach SAP before the order exists. Replaying the key republishes all of its parked events in their original order.

steps.label: circuit opens: pause partitions
steps.detail: The next calls fail fast with 503, so the breaker opens and the connector stops consuming instead of dead-lettering every order. Events pile up in Kafka with offsets uncommitted: about 8,300 orders and customer changes over 4 hours at the daily averages (3,300 orders plus 5,000 customer events), well inside 7 days of retention.

steps.label: orders not in ERP after 15 min
steps.detail: The business monitor sees the backlog. Inside the announced window it opens a ticket instead of paging, and after the window ends any stale order pages.

steps.label: half-open probe: GET $metadata
steps.detail: Once a minute the breaker lets one cheap call through to test whether SAP is back.

steps.label: resume, drain at 20 orders/s
steps.detail: At 20 events a second the backlog drains in about 7 minutes. The cap protects SAP's limited work processes, which a burst of thousands of parallel calls right after maintenance would overload.

steps.label: resolve api.acme.example
steps.detail: The support console finds API management by name; resolvers cache the answer, so this is rare.

steps.label: POST /ops/v1/replays
steps.detail: An integration engineer replays the dead-lettered order from the support console after checking the cause has gone.
steps.payload:
POST /ops/v1/replays HTTP/2
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci... (scope integration.replay)

{ "consumer": "erp-connector", "dlqTopic": "orders.erp-connector.dlq", "keys": ["SHOP-1002"],
  "reason": "SAP maintenance 2026-11-11, outcome unknown" }

steps.label: forward, scope checked
steps.detail: Replay can create business records, so only tokens with the replay scope get through, and every replay is written to an audit log with who, what and why.

steps.label: route /ops/* to an ops task
steps.detail: Same private hop: the load balancer routes /ops paths to the integration ops tasks.

steps.label: republish to orders.erp-connector.retry
steps.detail: The order goes to a retry topic that only the ERP connector reads, never back onto the main topic, where the WMS and CRM would receive it a second time. The original event id and headers are kept.

steps.label: claim event id
steps.detail: The claim finds the row from 02:00 still in_progress, so the connector knows an earlier attempt may have reached SAP.

steps.label: GET by PurchaseOrderByCustomer
steps.detail: Ask SAP, the system of record, rather than trust our own bookkeeping.

steps.label: found 4500012399
steps.detail: SAP had saved the order at 02:00:04, just before it shut down. A blind POST here would have created a duplicate order, a second invoice and possibly a second shipment.

steps.label: mark done, save xref, unpark key
steps.detail: Unparking lets new events for SHOP-1002 go straight to SAP again; any that were parked behind it arrive in the same replay, in order, after this one.

notes.text: At 5 events/s average this is not a throughput problem, so Kafka is chosen for per-key ordering, days of retention and replay from an offset, not speed. EventBridge or Pub/Sub without ordering keys would be simpler to run and is fine where order does not matter, but neither gives ordered replay of one key's history. Pub/Sub with ordering keys and seek is the closest managed middle ground on GCP.

Master data ownership is decided per field, not per record: the CRM owns customer contact details and consent, the ERP owns billing address, credit, tax, products and prices, the WMS owns stock on hand, and the shop owns the order until the ERP books it. Every connector writes only the fields its target owns, and producers publish only fields their system owns, which is also what prevents update loops.

The canonical model covers only the handful of events many systems share (OrderPlaced, CustomerUpdated, InventoryAdjusted), with N adapters to one model instead of N times N mappings. It is kept thin and versioned in the registry. A flow between exactly one producer and one consumer, such as warehouse labels to a carrier, maps directly; forcing it through an enterprise-wide model adds a committee and two mappings for no reuse.

A target that is down should pause its consumer and let lag build, because every message would fail the same way. The dead-letter topic is for messages that are wrong or whose outcome is unknown, not for a whole outage. Dead-lettering a message must also park its key, or later events for that key overtake it and break ordering.

BACKWARD compatibility (new readers can read old data) lets consumers upgrade first and is the usual default: adding an optional field with a default is allowed, renaming or removing a required field is rejected. A truly breaking change gets a new topic (orders.order-placed.v2) that the producer writes alongside the old one until every consumer has moved.

Partners get OAuth client credentials with per-partner scopes and quotas at API management. Inside, every connector has its own identity: its own OAuth client in SAP and Salesforce with a technical user limited to the objects it touches, its own Kafka ACLs (read its topics, write its retry and dead-letter topics), and its own secrets in Secrets Manager or Secret Manager, rotated automatically. One leaked credential then exposes one system, not all four.

The gateway is the only public entry, for partners and for the shop's webhooks, so it carries the web application firewall (managed rules, size limits, per-IP rate limits) in addition to per-partner OAuth and quotas. Webhook routes cannot use OAuth, so they are protected by the HMAC check in the adapter and, where the shop publishes its sending ranges, an IP allowlist. Behind the gateway nothing is public: the internal load balancer and the services sit in private subnets and accept traffic only from the gateway's private integration.

questions.q: Should the order process be choreographed through events, or orchestrated by a central workflow?
questions.a: Choreography fits here because the ERP, WMS and CRM react to OrderPlaced independently, and adding a fourth consumer needs no change to the producer. When steps depend on each other, such as the WMS needing the ERP delivery number or a refund that must undo several steps, an orchestrator (Step Functions, Workflows, Camunda) makes the sequence, timeouts and compensations explicit in one place. The cost of choreography is that nobody owns the end-to-end process, so you need business monitoring like the stale order check to see it.

questions.q: Why not keep point-to-point integrations, or put everything through a central ESB hub?
questions.a: Point-to-point is simplest for two systems but grows toward N times N links, each with its own mapping, retries and credentials, which is how the brittle scripts happened. A central ESB hub fixes the wiring but tends to collect business logic and become a bottleneck team that every change waits on. An event backbone with thin connectors, often called an event mesh when it spans brokers or clouds, keeps routing and delivery in the platform and business logic in the systems, with synchronous needs served separately through API management.

questions.q: What does a canonical data model buy you, and when would you not use one?
questions.a: It turns N times N mappings into N adapters to one shared model, gives events a stable contract that survives replacing a system, and lets the schema registry enforce compatibility. The risk is a bloated model that tries to hold every field of every system and needs a committee for each change. Keep it to the few widely shared business events with the fields consumers actually need, and map directly for flows with one producer and one consumer.

questions.q: Kafka supports exactly-once semantics. Why do the connectors still need dedup keys?
questions.a: Kafka's exactly-once covers reading from and writing to Kafka in one transaction; it cannot cover the side effect in SAP or Salesforce, and a timeout leaves that side effect unknown. So delivery is at least once and every consumer makes processing idempotent: a dedup row per event id, a natural key in the target (PurchaseOrderByCustomer, an external id upsert, a client order reference), and a lookup before creating whenever an earlier attempt is in doubt. Commit the offset only after the side effect, so a crash causes a repeat rather than a loss.

questions.q: On Black Friday the CRM connector starts hitting Salesforce API limits. What do you do?
questions.a: Read the remaining allowance from the Sforce-Limit-Info header and throttle with a token bucket set below it, because the org limit is shared with every other tool and user. Batch writes with the Composite or sObject Collections APIs (up to 200 records per call) or the Bulk API for large backfills, and drop low-value updates, such as coalescing several changes to one customer into one write. Since the work is queued in Kafka, slowing down only adds lag to the CRM, while the ERP and WMS are unaffected.

questions.q: A customer service agent says order SHOP-1002 is missing. How do you find it across five systems?
questions.a: Every event carries the order id as correlation id plus a W3C trace context, and every connector stamps the order tracking table when it succeeds, so one query shows which systems have it and when. The first missing stamp points to one connector: check its dead-letter topic and parked keys, its lag, then its logs by correlation id, and finally ask the target by external reference in case only the tracking update was lost. The 15-minute stale order alert should have found it before the customer did.
